chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Sulayman ibn Khalid, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
If your camel gives birth, milk it for a time that does not harm its offspring, then sacrifice both (the mother and the offspring).
I asked: 'Do I drink from its milk and give others to drink?' He said: 'Yes.'
And he said: 'Indeed, Ali, Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him), when he saw people walking who were exhausted by walking, would carry them upon his sacrificial camels.'
And he said: 'If a man's mount strays or perishes, and with him is a sacrificial animal (hady), let him ride upon his sacrificial animal.'

key_terms.أَمِيرَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ: Commander of the Faithful (title for Imam Ali)
key_terms.انْحَرْهُمَا: Sacrifice both (referring to the mother and the newborn)
key_terms.بَدَنَتُكَ: Your sacrificial camel (specifically a female camel used for sacrifice)
key_terms.هَدْيٌ: Sacrificial animal brought by a pilgrim or traveler

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on milking and riding a sacrificial camel that gives birth or is used by travelers?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi establishes the permissibility of milking a sacrificial camel (badanah) that gives birth, provided the offspring is not harmed, and mandates sacrificing both mother and young, reflecting the Shafi'i and Hanbali views in contrast to the Hanafi position. It further illustrates the practical flexibility (rukhas) in Hajj rituals through the example of Imam Ali (peace be upon him), who permitted riding the sacrificial animal if the primary mount failed, emphasizing the principle of removing hardship in religious obligations.
